- **Category:** missing gate / derived facts restated as prose
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** AUD-149 fix, sibling sweep (asking why a table this visible stayed wrong for a week)

**Evidence before.** AUD-149 is the defect; this row is the reason it could happen. Four current files state the size of the gate set: `AGENTS.md` says thirteen, `RELEASE.md` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:109` said twelve, and `docs/handover-tinytitan.md` said twelve in its paste block - while `tools/lint.sh` ran fourteen after AUD-142 and AUD-151 each added a gate on 2026-10-06. Measured by mutation: with both counts typed back to `twelve`, `tools/lint.sh` still exits 0 - no gate reads a document - so the only thing that keeps such a sentence true is the person who happens to notice. The same shape appears in citations: the brief and AUD-106's own record named `v5.18` -> `d30de44`, `v5.17` -> `1904be4`, `v5.16` -> `0fd9df2`, but `git cat-file -t` on all three says `tag`, and the tagged commits are `ea5de8c`, `701bb2e`, `551522a`. A commit sha is the key `tools/ci-green.sh`, `tools/release.sh` and `gh run list --commit` need, so a reader following the citation gets a tag stanza and no run. Both are the same failure: a fact the repository can compute is restated in prose, and prose does not fail when the computation changes. Note the difference from AUD-151's file-length case - there the number was a *standard*; here the numbers and shas are *derived values*, so the fix is not to enforce a limit but to forbid restating a derivable fact where it can be generated or checked. | 2026-10-07 addendum, measured while closing AUD-128: a fourth gate has landed since this row was filed (test-hollow, 15th), and the drift this row describes is now asymmetric rather than uniform -- RELEASE.md and ci.yml's step name were edited in the same commit as the gate, as RELEASE.md's own rule requires, while AGENTS.md still says "thirteen checks" and its mode list omits both file-length and test-hollow (it names two of the four gates this audit added). The gate count appears in four places and exactly one of them is derived from tools/lint.sh; the other three are typed by hand. Nothing compares them, which is the whole of this row.

**Fix.** `tools/lint.sh docs` (17th gate): `tools/docs-facts.py` derives the gate set from `tools/lint.sh` itself -- the `all)` chain, the `case` arms, the usage header and the unknown-check message, cross-checked against each other before any document is judged -- then compares every tracked `*.md`/`*.yml` against it: count claims (`N checks|gates` anchored to `tools/lint.sh`/`CI`), mode names that answer to nothing, restated audit-ledger `counts`, and `tag -> sha` citations verified with `git rev-parse tag^{commit}`. Excluded by rule, not by exemption list: history sections (`## What has landed`), dated run records (`all fifteen gates ok`), unanchored numbers, quoted retired values, and this audit's own ledger + release notes -- a document that records what it corrected must keep the wrong value to be readable, and this audit corrects forward. `AGENTS.md` is printed as OWNER and never fails the gate: it is the maintainer's file, being edited outside this session, and a red CI hostage by it teaches nobody anything. Writing it found two more live defects, both fixed here: four documented mode names (`unchecked-sendable`, `silent-test-skip`, `shell-portability`, `shell-lint`) were not runnable and are now aliases with every spelling in the unknown-check message, and two paths in the new script crashed with a traceback instead of reporting a verdict (missing `tools/lint.sh`, `ROOT` not a directory). The five documents the gate named are fixed: `CONTRIBUTING.md` (eleven -> seventeen, its stale single-gate list replaced by a pointer to the usage header) and the handover's three count claims plus its restated ledger counts. Extended at c482ad8 after the gate's own blind spot bit its author: `check_tables()` counts unescaped `|` per row of any header/separator/body block and compares it to the header, because a row with the wrong cell count renders as a table that silently drops or pads cells -- an edit to the handover that this gate had just forced added a trailing pipe, `tools/lint.sh docs` still read the file as clean, and only reading the line back found it. The GFM escape rule is the gate's, not an exemption: `\|` is a literal pipe, which is why `docs/release-process.md`'s `pgrep` row is correct at nine pipes (a first version of the check called it a defect, so that shape is now a pinned arm). Two probe arms that were anchored to sentences the documents may change are located from the file at run time now.

**Evidence after.** `tools/lint.sh docs` exits 0: `ok (82 documents against 17 gates derived from tools/lint.sh; 1 owner-file note(s) reported and not enforced)`, the one note being `AGENTS.md:250`'s count. Measured before the fix on this tree: rc=1 with 5 FAILs -- `CONTRIBUTING.md:24` eleven, `docs/handover-tinytitan.md:23/128/132` fifteen, and that file's `60 rows / 53 closed / 6 open / 1 blocked` against the ledger's 61/57/3/1 -- plus `OWNER AGENTS.md:250`. The four aliases were run: `tools/lint.sh unchecked-sendable|silent-test-skip|shell-portability|shell-lint` all exit 0 (each exited 2 before, and `shell-portability` is the exact name `AGENTS.md` teaches). Mutation proof committed as `docs/audit-2026-10-06/AUD-160-docs-probe.py`: 18/18 arms -- ten that must fail (wrong count, dead mode name, off-by-one ledger counts, tag-object sha, a plain wrong sha, header label with no `case` arm, chain entry with no arm, a mode omitted from `--help`, and the two crash paths), four that must not (a wrong count under a history heading, a dated run record, an unanchored number, a quoted retired value), and the two revert arms that show the tree came back byte-identical with the gate green. The two table arms: a row with one cell too many fails with both column counts named, and a row of `\|` escapes inside a code span passes -- plus `docs/release-process.md`'s live nine-pipe row, which the baseline run covers. Both commits were verified on their own tree: with `ledger.json` and the handover at `260a925`'s values, `tools/lint.sh docs` exits 0 and the probe reads 18/18, so no commit in this chain leaves a document disagreeing with the repository it describes.

**Evidence before.** The same mistake, elsewhere, measured 2026-10-06: `AGENTS.md:268` and `CONTRIBUTING.md:37` each state `14 rows` for `tools/func-length-baseline.txt`, and the handover's Goldens row states `16 files under benchmark/golden/` and `16 targets in `tools/golden-baseline.sh`. All four are true right now -- `wc -l` says 14, `git ls-files benchmark/golden | wc -l` says 16 -- so this is not a live wrong number, it is the class AUD-160 exists to end left half-covered: a gate that added its own row to `tools/func-length-baseline.txt` or a golden target would silently stale these sentences exactly the way `library-facade` staled the gate counts on 2026-10-07. `tools/docs-facts.py` compares only the counts it can derive without a second parser today.

**Fix.** `tools/docs-facts.py` gained `check_derived_counts`, which judges three more restated counts against the tree: `N rows` attributed to the nearest `tools/*.txt` within 300 characters (compared with that file's non-blank line count), `N files under `dir`` (compared with `git ls-files dir`), and `N targets in `tools/golden-baseline.sh`` (compared with the target list that script's own `unknown target:` message prints). Each is matched by phrase and must name the file or directory it is a claim about, because the bare pattern `N rows|files|targets` also matches an n-gram table (48 rows per token), a git diff (353 files, 10 files changed) and a locale catalogue (3,633 rows x 2 locales): 23 hits in the corpus, four of them claims about this tree. `N rows / N closed` is left to `check_ledger_counts`, which is the check that owns it. The window is 300 characters rather than the whole paragraph because CONTRIBUTING.md's gate list is one paragraph, and a claim in its last bullet would otherwise inherit the first bullet's file. Quoted numbers stay mentions and history headings stay dated, on the same rules AUD-160 set. While proving the arm for a count whose file does not exist, the table check was widened to every tracked document rather than the 82 the number checks may read -- a mis-shaped row is a rendering defect, not a quotation of history -- and it immediately found one in the file that documents the gates: `tool-coverage.md:205`, the `library-facade` row, carried a fourth column in a three-column table. Fixed in the same commit (`28fd719`); no row is filed for it because nothing is open after it.

### AUD-170 — `ttlanmanager --key` puts the group key in argv, where every other local account reads it with ps, and nothing said so

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier A
- **Project:** fleet
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift:115 (was the inline `??` chain), sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift`
- **Category:** secret through a world-visible channel, on the one path where the secret is the operator's own
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L4 sweep's leftover question about how the fleet key is carried

**Evidence before.** The shipped default `tinytitan-lan` is public by design -- `router.js:101` tells a peer that presents it that the key `groups rather than protects`, and that is the right reading of a default. So the key that matters is the one an operator chose *because* they want other people out, and the documented way to pass it to the CLI is `--key`, which is also the first name in the resolution order the help text prints. macOS shows every account's argv to every other account through `ps`; a process's environment belongs to its own user. The help line named the order and never named the difference, and the README's own habit of writing the token into a `curl -H` argument goes out the same door. Nothing in the tree said which spelling to prefer.

**Fix.** The resolution moves out of the executable's top-level code into `FleetGroupKey` -- `FleetKey` was already taken by the keyboard enum in `FleetDashboard.swift` -- with the order untouched, and returns the warning alongside the key. `--key` now puts one line on stderr naming the channel and pointing at `DSH_LAN_KEY`, and the usage text says the same before anyone types it. Errors and warnings go to stderr, so `--json` output stays parseable.

**Evidence after.** Measured 2026-10-06. 2 tests in `tests/TinyTitanFleet/KeySourceTests.swift` pin both the warning and the order (a reorder would change which key a machine presents without touching any other assertion). Fleet suite 51 tests in 13 suites passed. Mutation probe: with the warning replaced by `nil` the test fails with two named issues, so the probe is not a compile check. Live: `swift run ttlanmanager --key probe-key --peer 127.0.0.1:59999 --timeout 1 inventory` prints the line on stderr before dialling anything, and the executable builds under `-warnings-as-errors`. NOT covered as filed: the same literal lives in `plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js` as `DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY` and nothing pinned the two together -- a Swift test reaching into `plugins/` has no precedent here, and inventing one was not this row's call. AUD-175 (c3b3a84) closed it from the other side, in `tools/docs-facts.py`, which is allowed to read both languages.

**Commit.** `a9bd232`

### AUD-171 — An unexpected throw answers with its own message, so a filesystem failure names this Mac's paths to any peer that can reach the port

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier B
- **Project:** plugins
- **Location:** `plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/router.js:326 (the catch-all), plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/api.js:800 (the session-controller wrapper)`
- **Category:** internal detail in an error answer, plus a mislabelled status on the sibling site
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L4 pass over what the manager says when it fails

**Evidence before.** The router's catch-all answered 500 with `error.message` verbatim. The throws that reach it are the unexpected ones -- `node:fs` and child-process failures -- and Node puts the absolute path in their messages, so the answer told any caller where this Mac keeps its profiles. The manager listens on the LAN by design, so "any caller" is not only this user. One layer down sat the same defect with a second problem: the session-controller wrapper wrapped *any* throw into an `ApiError` carrying its message, so that route never passed through the router fence at all, and its fallback gave an uncoded controller failure status 400 -- telling the caller to fix a request that was fine.

**Fix.** The catch-all keeps the log line that already recorded the stack and answers with a fixed message that says where the detail is. `ApiError` messages still go out unchanged, because those are authored here and are the documented answer for a known failure. The wrapper now keeps the code and message only of an error the controller *authored* -- one carrying its own code -- and rethrows anything else to the catch-all, which both logs it and calls it a 500.

**Evidence after.** Measured 2026-10-06. `an unexpected throw answers a fixed 500 and keeps its detail in the log` asserts the absence of the path and the presence of the log line, so the fix cannot become a silent failure. On the unfixed sources it fails with `expected: 500` and an actual of 400 -- the path was in the body at that point. Suite 130 pass / 0 fail; the 501 case and the `workspace/not-found` case still assert their authored messages, which is the half that had to survive. NOT covered as filed: the fan-out receipts in `prompt-all` and the archive path echo per-session failure messages, and api.js has no logger in scope to put the detail anywhere else -- fixing that needs a log channel threaded through, not a message swapped. That is what AUD-174 (cf2088d) then did, at all six sites this class has here.

**Commit.** `fe467d9`

### AUD-173 — The peer prober's fan-out bound is applied but pinned by no test, so deleting it leaves the whole suite green

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier A
- **Project:** fleet
- **Location:** `plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/peers.js:435 (the untested limit argument)`
- **Category:** unpinned guard (missing test)
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L6 closure sweep, while checking whether AUD-168's NOT-covered sentence was still true

**Evidence before.** AUD-168 closed the size of one peer's answer and said the number of concurrent probes was not covered. It is covered by code: `#refresh()` fans probes out through `mapLimit(validated, this.config.discoveryConcurrency ?? DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, ...)` (peers.js:433-437) with `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY = 24` (:36), and the resolution phase runs on its own shallower `?? 4` (:417) which does have a test (test/peers.test.js:312-333). What had no witness was the argument at :435: `mapLimit` itself is tested for bound and order (:79-95), and `discoveryConcurrency` is validated in config.js:216-218, but nothing asserted that either reaches the probe fan-out. Mutation-measured: replacing that expression with `validated.length` leaves all 130 other tests in the file passing while the resident manager dials every candidate the fence admits at once -- 24 sockets held open per cycle becomes as many as discovery returns.

**Fix.** One test that counts peak in-flight fetches across a refresh: over 40 candidates with no configured limit it must be exactly `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY`, and over 12 with `discoveryConcurrency: 3` it must be exactly 3. The second case is what makes the first mean "the configured limit is applied" rather than "some number happened to be peak"; `===` rather than `<=` because a bound that silently became 1 would be a different defect (a cycle that never finishes) and an inequality would let it pass as a success.

**Evidence after.** Measured 2026-10-06. With `peers.js:435` mutated to `validated.length` the new test fails (peak 40, expected 24) and is the only failure; `src/peers.js` was then restored from a copy taken before the edit and `git diff` reports no change, i.e. the committed source is untouched -- only the test file is in the commit. Full suites after: dsh-lan-manager `npm test` 131 passed / 0 failed, `tools/lint.sh javascript` ok.

**Commit.** `b3c1916`

### AUD-174 — The sites AUD-171 left open answer a LAN peer with the harness's own failure text, and the one that meant to keep only authored failures admits a Node error code

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier B
- **Project:** plugins
- **Location:** `plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/api.js:547,563,692,743,847 (the interpolated messages) and :814 (the authored-code test)`
- **Category:** internal detail in an error answer (information disclosure)
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L6 closure sweep, following the NOT-covered sentence filed in the AUD-173 row, which named exactly these sites

**Evidence before.** At 9c98268 six places put a failure this process did not author into an answer any peer inside the address fence can ask for. `derivedMessagesFromStore` interpolated the caught error's message into two 503s (`…could not be read from storage: ENOENT…` at :547, `…could not be prepared for reading: ENOENT…` at :563); `promptAllActive`'s per-session receipt carried it verbatim (:692); `deleteWorkspace`'s `archiveFailures` carried it with no code at all (:741-744); `createWorkspace` answered 400 with the caught message as the whole answer (:845-848). The sixth is the same class in a different shape: `startSession` keeps a caught error's code and message when `typeof error?.code === "string"` (:814) -- and a Node error has a string `code` too (`ENOENT`, `EACCES`), so a failed spawn's `child_process` text goes out labelled a caller's bad request. Reproduced, not argued: the seven tests added with this fix were run against `git show 9c98268:` copies of `src/api.js` and `src/router.js` (swapped in, restored afterwards, tree confirmed clean) and 6 of 7 fail there with the leak printed in the assertion output -- e.g. `{"error":"agent-service-unavailable","message":"session s-a1 could not be read from storage: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/Users/me/.dsh/home/profiles/web/s-a1.json'"}`, `{"sessionId":"s-b1","code":"error","message":"ENOENT: …s-b1.json"}`, and `400 !== 500` for the spawn failure. AUD-171 had already recorded that these sites were left open because none of them held a logger.

**Fix.** One rule, applied at all six: the code and the status are the documented answer and stay; the reason goes to the manager's log. `loggedApiError` builds the ApiError from a sentence authored here plus `; the reason is in the manager's log`, and `loggedReceipt` does the same for a fan-out entry while keeping that failure's declared `code` -- which also gives `archiveFailures` a code it never had. The log channel is threaded `createHandler` -> `dispatch` -> the four operations as a **separate trailing `plumbing` argument**, not inside `options`: `options` is the request body's shape and a peer must not be able to hand the plugin a function. `startSession`'s authored-code test becomes `isDocumentedCode`, which accepts the lowercase-hyphen, optionally namespaced vocabulary this plugin and the harness actually emit (`not-found`, `workspace/not-found`, `session-busy`) and rethrows an uppercase Node code so the router's catch-all logs it and answers a fixed 500 -- the status also stops calling an internal failure the caller's bad request. The message rule is now written down in the plugin README's Security section, next to the key-never-in-a-response rule.

**Evidence after.** Measured 2026-10-07 on commit cf2088d. Seven tests in `test/router.test.js`: one per leaking site, and each of those six asserts the answer carries no `/Users/me` **and** that the reason reached the injected log -- so a guard that only moved the leak would still fail. The seventh is the counter-test, deliberately passing before and after -- `an authored ApiError still says what it means inside a fan-out` asserts `session s-a2 has no live agent (start it in the UI, then retry)` still arrives, because fencing somebody else's text must not turn every answer into a shrug; it is why the negative probe shows 6 failures and not 7. Suite: `npm test` in dsh-lan-manager reports 138 tests / 138 pass / 0 fail (was 131 before these seven), dsh-tinytitan 154/154, and `tools/lint.sh javascript` reports ok for both packages on the pinned eslint 10.11.0 / prettier 3.9.9. The negative probe is above; after restoring, `git status --short` on the package is empty and both files matched their pre-probe checksums.

**Commit.** `cf2088d`

### AUD-175 — The shipped fleet group key is one value written in two languages, and a drift between them empties every peer table without failing any gate

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier A
- **Project:** docs-gates
- **Location:** `tools/docs-facts.py: shared_group_key(), called from main(). The two definitional sites it reads: sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift:20 (shippedDefault) and plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js:54 (DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY)`
- **Category:** two sources of truth for one identity fact, with prose as the only link
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L6 closure sweep, following the NOT-covered sentence filed in the AUD-170 row, which named this literal and the JS one beside it

**Evidence before.** Written twice by necessity, pinned by nothing. `FleetGroupKey.shippedDefault` is `"tinytitan-lan"` in Swift and `DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY` is the same string in the plugin's `config.js`, because one Mac runs the CLI and the harness side against one LAN and an unconfigured install must present the *same key* to both. The only link was prose: the Swift doc comment's "the two literals here have to move with it" and the resolution-order row in `config.js`'s module header. The consequence of moving one is quiet, not loud. A member names its group by a digest of the key it presents (`groupDigest`, AUD-154), so a machine on the changed default computes a different digest, `router.js` answers it as a foreign group, and the peer table empties -- no error, no non-zero exit, nothing in a log that says *your fleet has no members because your default moved*. Measured on the pre-fix tree (8686e9e): with `config.js` edited to `"tinytitan-la"` -- one character short of the Swift literal -- `python3 tools/docs-facts.py` printed `ok (83 documents against 17 gates ...)` and exited 0. Every gate here reads either its own language or its own file; none had ever looked at both.

**Fix.** `shared_group_key()` in the docs gate reads both definitional sites by pattern, not by quoting a value into a document, and returns a row for each way it can go wrong: `FAIL cannot read <rel> for the group key: ...`, `FAIL <rel>: no shipped default group key matched <pattern>`, and `FAIL the shipped group key has two values: <site> = <value>; ...`. The middle one is the important shape -- a renamed or reformatted declaration fails the gate instead of leaving a site unchecked, which is the rule this file already applies to its own counter (`docs` reports a failure when it derived no gates). Both literals now carry a line naming the pin, and the `docs` bullet in `AGENTS.md` says the gate reads a value defined in two languages, so the next person who edits one finds the fence before the drift.

**Evidence after.** Measured 2026-10-07 on commit c3b3a84. Two mutation probes, each failing observably, each restored and verified by checksum with `git status` clean afterwards. Drifting the JS literal by one character: `FAIL the shipped group key has two values: plugins/dsh-lan-manager/src/config.js = 'tinytitan-la'; sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift = 'tinytitan-lan'`. Re-spelling the Swift declaration as `public static let shippedDefault: String = { "tinytitan-lan" }()`, which compiles and behaves identically: `FAIL sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetGroupKey.swift: no shipped default group key matched static let shippedDefault = "([^"]+)"` -- so the check cannot be quietly disarmed by editing its own pattern out of the source. Restored tree: `docs` ok on 83 documents against 17 derived gates, exit 0. `python` (ruff 0.16.7, parses under 3.13), `swift-format`, `swiftlint --strict`, `file-length` (largest 496) and `javascript` (eslint 10.11.0 + prettier 3.9.9, suite 138 pass / 0 fail) clean; `swift build` and the Fleet suite (51 tests in 13 suites, `--no-parallel`) pass. NOT covered: the check pins the two *shipped defaults* to each other, not either to the fleet's real configuration -- an operator who sets `DSH_LAN_KEY` on some members and not others still gets an empty peer table, correctly, and no gate here can know which keys were meant to match. Also not covered: `config.js:166`'s resolution order (`groupKey ?? token ?? DSH_LAN_KEY ?? DSH_LAN_TOKEN ?? DEFAULT_GROUP_KEY`) is the mirror of the Swift order AUD-170 pinned in `KeySourceTests.swift`, and the two orders are still kept in step by reading them, not by a check.

**Commit.** `c3b3a84`

### AUD-180 — The engine's opt-in traces write stdout through the library, and rule 1's gate only ever looked at the library's own directory

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier C
- **Project:** lint-gates
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitan/Runtime/Inference/RealForwardRunner+PrefillLayer.swift:220-236 and RealForwardRunner+DecodeMoE.swift:479-493 (the writes); tools/lint.sh:659 check_library_stdout (the gate)`
- **Category:** documented contract with no gate over the code that actually implements it
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** the L7/§6 sweep for code the facade promise does not cover: `AGENTS.md` rule 1 says nothing in the library may `print` because "stdout belongs to the embedding program", and the hunt for where that promise is enforced led to `tools/library-facade-rules.py`, which walks `os.walk(sources/TinyTitanLib)` and nothing else

**Evidence before.** The promise was met in the letter and missed in the purpose. `library-facade-rules.py:22,35` sets LIB to sources/TinyTitanLib and walks that directory, so the 33 files it scans clean is 33 files out of the 211 an embedder actually links: TinyTitanLib depends on TinyTitan, TinyTitanFormat and TinyTitanKernelsC, and every library call runs through the engine. Six stdout writes sat in that unreachable part of the graph, all in RealForwardRunner: the prefill phase trace under TURBO_FIELDFARE_PHASES (PrefillLayer.swift:222, 223, 226, 229, 233 -- five `print` calls, five lines) and the decode layer trace under TINYTITAN_LAYER_TRACE (DecodeMoE.swift:485). Both are opt-in, which is why they survived: the CLI is the only front end that has ever set them, and a CLI owns its stdout. An embedder that set one got trace text interleaved with its own answers -- the exact failure rule 1 exists to prevent -- and nothing in the tree would have caught the next one, because no gate read the closure.

**Fix.** Both traces now write stderr, with every label kept exactly as `docs/cpu-coexecution-plan.md:1021-1027` quotes them (route readback + GPU, expert fetch + tiles, tail + residual, active experts/layer), through the runtime's own idiom (`FileHandle.standardError.write(Data(...utf8))`, as at PreadExpertStreamer.swift:61). The message is bound to an explicitly typed `let trace: String` first: the same concatenation inlined in `Data((...).utf8)` did not type-check in reasonable time, and that failure was a build error, not a style choice. Eighteenth gate `stdout-clean` enforces the rule over the closure `Package.swift` gives `TinyTitanLib`, resolving targets and `dependencies:` arrays from the manifest by balancing its brackets, so a dependency enters the gate on the commit it enters the library; the opt-out is `lint:allow-stdout <reason>`.

**Evidence after.** RED before any source change: `tools/lint.sh stdout-clean` on the unmodified tree exited 1 naming exactly the six sites predicted from reading the two env-gated blocks -- the gate's first run was the finding. GREEN after: exit 0, `ok (4 targets in TinyTitanLib's closure, 211 Swift files, no stdout write)`. Ten probe arms, recorded in `docs/audit-2026-10-06/tool-coverage.md`: a bare `print` in a closure target exits 1 naming file, line and call; the same site with `lint:allow-stdout <reason>` above it exits 0; the file reverted, `git status` back to only this change's files and the gate green again; and in a copied tree with a synthetic manifest, the three measured-nothing guards each exit 1 (root target renamed out of `Package.swift`, a declared `path:` that does not exist, closure directories holding no `.swift`), a `print` in the dependency is caught while a `print` in a target that depends *on* the library is not -- proving the walk follows `dependencies:` and that a front end keeps its stdout. Text-preservation check: the string-literal fragments of both blocks diffed `HEAD` against the working tree compare identical once newline placement is normalised (19 and 13 fragments, no content change). `swift build -c release` exit 0 with zero errors and zero warnings under `-warnings-as-errors`, after the inlined-concatenation type-check failure was fixed. Full chain `tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 with zero FAIL lines across 18 gate headers, `docs` printing `ok (83 documents against 18 gates derived from tools/lint.sh, table shape in all 109; 0 owner-file note(s))`. Four documents restated the old count and the gate named all four: CONTRIBUTING.md:24, the handover's gate row, its audit row and its CI row. Sibling sweep: the C target in the closure was checked for the same mistake through a channel the Swift-only scanner cannot see (`printf`/`fputs`/`stdout` in sources/TinyTitanKernelsC -- none), and the 91 remaining stdout writes in sources/ were located in 14 files, every one an executable outside the closure, so the scope is neither narrower than the promise nor wider than it should be. The gate count itself needed no restating anywhere else: `docs-facts.py` derives it from the `all)` chain.

### AUD-181 — Four public prefill diagnostics types have had no producer since the Mac app was removed; the only thing keeping them compile-checked is a test of the types themselves

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier C
- **Project:** runtime
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitan/Runtime/Prefill/PrefillRuntimeConfig.swift:117-177 (the four types), tests/TinyTitan/Runtime/Prefill/PrefillRuntimeConfigTests.swift:diagnosticsPreserveUnknownValues (their only consumer)`
- **Category:** surface wired to nothing, kept reachable by its own test (§6)
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** §6 unused-code sweep (identifier-token counter over sources/ + tests/, then a manual read of every candidate)

**Evidence before.** Verified against the tree before filing, not from the sweep's report. The sweep flagged the four names declared in PrefillRuntimeConfig.swift -- PrefillKVStorageMode, PrefillExecutedMode, PrefillChunkCompleteness, PrefillExecutionDiagnostics -- and the manual read confirmed it: every remaining mention sits inside their own definitions, plus one test (`diagnosticsPreserveUnknownValues`) that constructs a PrefillExecutionDiagnostics and asserts it still holds the values handed to its initialiser. A test that can only fail if the struct forgets its own stored properties does not exercise the engine. `git grep -l PrefillExecutionDiagnostics 3d33d4b^` names six files: the definition, that test, and four real consumers -- sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Diagnostics/AppDiagnostics.swift, sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Inference/DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift, sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Inference/RealInferenceClient.swift and sources/TinyTitanDecodeService/DecodeServiceOutbox.swift. `3d33d4b scope: remove the Mac app; the product is the engine and its server` (2026-09-17) deleted those four and left the vocabulary behind; `git log -S` shows it arrived with `6b9070f The First Flight of TurboFieldfare` (2026-07-19), the same commit as the app. So the runtime has carried 61 lines of public API nothing reads for 21 days, and no engine, CLI, server or library path ever populated an executed-mode or chunk-completeness value. Nothing in the tree prints, serialises or compares one.

**Fix.** Deleted the four types and the test that existed only for them: 73 lines across two files, no other file touched, no behaviour changed because no behaviour referenced them. The runtime config the prefill planner does use -- PrefillRuntimeConfig, PrefillChunkSpan, PrefillChunkPlanner and their tests -- is untouched, and the two tests that cover the live planner (including the long-Qwen chunk case) still pass. `sources/TinyTitan/Runtime/Prefill/PrefillRuntimeConfig.swift` goes from 215 to 153 lines. The `PrefillKVStorageMode` bridge from KVCachePrecision went with it; the cache precision type itself is live and unchanged.

**Evidence after.** Measured after the deletion, every command's exit code read directly rather than through a pipe: `swift build -c release` exits 0 with zero `error:` and zero `warning:` lines. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel` exits 0 -- 1695 tests in 252 suites passed across seven test runs (796/127, 395/47, 148/22, 176/23, 35/10, 51/13, 94/10), one test fewer than the 1696 before, which is exactly the test deleted, and zero failures. `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH ./tools/lint.sh all` exits 0 with zero FAIL lines across all eighteen gates. A tree-wide Grep for `PrefillExecutionDiagnostics|PrefillKVStorageMode|PrefillExecutedMode|PrefillChunkCompleteness` returns no matches, so no doc, comment or plugin names them either. THE LIMITATION, stated rather than papered over: no automated guard catches an orphan type, and this fix does not add one -- a compiler cannot, because a public declaration that compiles is legal, and a `references <= 2` gate would have failed on ten other §6 candidates that all proved used. The §6 sweep is the control for this class, which is why the sweep also records that the tree holds little other dead public API. The sibling question -- what else the app removal left behind -- was answered by the same command rather than by assumption: `git grep -l <name> 3d33d4b^` for each of the other three returns a subset of the same six files (PrefillKVStorageMode and PrefillExecutedMode: the definition plus `DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift` and `RealInferenceClient.swift`; PrefillChunkCompleteness: the definition plus `DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift`), so every consumer of every one of the four lived in the app or the decode service and the island went together. It also caught one thing the row does not claim: `AppDiagnostics.swift` and `DecodeServiceOutbox.swift` referenced only PrefillExecutionDiagnostics, not the other three, so the six-file list is the union and not each type's own consumer set.

**Commit.** `0038abf`

### AUD-183 — The fleet command line documents two options it does not mention, discards a number it cannot read, and ignores an option it does not know -- including the one flag that protects a delete from archiving every session

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier B
- **Project:** fleet
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift:64-78 (the option block), :65 (`--timeout ... .flatMap(Double.init) ?? 10`), :92 (the command word is taken and the rest never re-checked)`
- **Category:** integrity / fail-silent argument handling: undocumented surface, malformed value defaulted silently, unknown option dropped
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** L3 line-level pass over the fleet executable's argument block, after AUD-182 put that file under the microscope; the same class AUD-178 found in the installer, seen from the other side (there a documented flag was never read; here a read flag was never documented).

**Evidence before.** Measured against the shipped binary before filing, with exit codes read straight from the process. (1) Undocumented surface: `--base-path` (main.swift:64, default `/dsh-lan`, threaded into every request path in FleetClient) and `--interval` (:78, used by `top` at :275 as `max(2, intervalOption ?? 30)`) are parsed and honoured but appear nowhere in `--help`; comparing the two sets over the built help output and the parser gives parsed-but-undocumented `[--base-path, --help, --interval]` and documented-but-never-parsed `[]`. (2) Silent default: `--timeout ten workspace create --path DIR --on probehost` against a stub member exits 0 with `ok` -- the value was thrown away and the default used; the control proves the flag is otherwise honoured, because `--timeout 0.000001 workspace create ...` exits 1 with `127.0.0.1:39851 is unreachable: The request timed out.` The same `.flatMap(Double.init)`/`.flatMap(Int.init) ?? default` shape covers `--limit`, `--concurrency`, `--width`, `--height` and `--interval`. (3) Ignored option: after the command word every unrecognised token is dropped without a trace -- `workspace create --base-pathz /nope --path DIR --on probehost` exits 0 `ok`, and `list --peer-override 1.2.3.4` exits 0 and lists the local group. The destructive instance is the one that matters: `workspace delete --workspace ID --keep-session` (one `s` short) deletes the workspace *and* archives its sessions, because `keepSessions` was never set and the flag that was meant to set it was ignored. Reach: nothing in-tree invokes `ttlanmanager` -- `grep -rn ttlanmanager plugins tools benchmark` returns three comments in the plugin's router and test file, no call -- so tightening the parser cannot break a caller here. The sibling sweep found this class already fixed everywhere else, which is what makes the fleet CLI a gap rather than a house style: `tools/server_launcher.sh:261` answers `-*) echo "unknown option: $1 (try --help)"; exit 2`, `TinyTitanCLI/Args.swift:111` and `ServerArguments.swift:343` throw `unknown flag`, `TinyTitanRepack/Command/main.swift:177` throws `unknown argument`, `tests/TinyTitan/CLI/CLIArgumentsTests.swift:193` (`helpListsExactlyThePublicOptions`) pins the CLI's help against the exact option set, and `tinytitan-memory` documents both flags it takes and fails safe on a typo'd one -- its `forget` requires `--yes` to be *recognised*, so `--ye` refuses instead of deleting.

**Fix.** Three halves, all in the argument layer. `--help` moved to the core library as `FleetUsage.text` -- pure code motion, and the move is verified rather than asserted: the help output is byte-identical before and after (`shasum -a 256` of `ttlanmanager --help` on both trees, both `c308904e...`), which is the point of an unimportable target's strings -- and it now documents `--base-path`, `--interval` and `--help`, with the key-resolution paragraph re-wrapped, since the previous sentence had been broken mid-clause by an earlier edit. A numeric option is read by `numberOption`, which fails the run naming the flag and the text (`--timeout needs a number, ten`); it also rejects the spellings `Double.init` accepts and no operator means -- `nan`, `inf` -- because a NaN timeout is not a timeout. Anything left in `arguments` after the command word is read is refused as `unknown option: X`, the launcher's wording, before any request goes out. No option's *default* changed: `--timeout` is still 10 s, `--concurrency` still 4, `top`'s interval still 30 s floored at 2, `--base-path` still `/dsh-lan`.

**Evidence after.** TDD, in that order. The suite went in first: `swift test --no-parallel --filter FleetUsageTests` exits 1 with three tests and six issues, each a real expectation and not a crash -- `undocumented.isEmpty` false, `bad.stderr.contains("--timeout")` false, `contains("ten")` false, `contains("--interval")` false, `contains("--keep-session")` false, `contains("--not-an-option")` false (`/tmp/red183.log`). The first version of the guard's source scan over-read -- it took the `--keep-session` in the *comment* about the typo for a parse site, so the assertion was measuring prose; the scan now matches only a source literal that is exactly an option name, which is what a parser reads, and the narrowed rule still reproduces the filed gap on the pre-fix help output (`--base-path, --help, --interval` undocumented, nothing phantom). After the fix the filter exits 0, 3 tests in 1 suite: `helpNamesEveryOptionTheParserReads` asserts both directions against the *built* executable's own `--help` and the parser's own source, `anUnreadableNumberIsRefusedNotSilentlyDefaulted` covers `--timeout`, `--interval` and the valid-value control that proves the refusal is about the text, and `anOptionNobodyReadsIsAnErrorNotASilence` pins the `--keep-session` typo and a stray option. `swift build -c release` exits 0 with no warning and the full serial suite exits 0 at 1701 tests in 253 suites; `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exits 0 across all 18 gates. Re-measured live on the rebuilt release binary against a stub member on 127.0.0.1:39861, exit codes read straight from the process (`/tmp/probe183.out`): `workspace create --path DIR --peer ... --on probehost` -> `ok`, exit 0; the same with `--base-path /dsh-lan` -> `ok`, exit 0, so the newly documented flag is honoured, not merely named; `--timeout ten` -> exit 1 `--timeout needs a number, not ten`; `--timeout nan` -> exit 1 `--timeout needs a finite number, not nan`; `--interval soon top --once` -> exit 1 `--interval needs a number, not soon`; `--base-pathz /nope` -> exit 1 `unknown option: --base-pathz`; `list --peer-override 1.2.3.4` -> exit 1 `unknown option: --peer-override`; `workspace delete --workspace ws-new --keep-session` -> exit 1 `unknown option: --keep-session`, which is the destructive case and it now refuses before any request goes out; `list --not-an-option` -> exit 1; and the control `--timeout 0.000001 workspace create ...` -> exit 1 `127.0.0.1:39861 is unreachable: The request timed out.`, proving a readable timeout is still obeyed. Release `--help` exits 0 and its option set against the parser's is 21 options with `[]` undocumented and `[]` phantom. Sibling answer and its limit: the guard is a test that reads `sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift` by `#filePath` and spawns `.build/debug/ttlanmanager`, both idioms already used here (`SideEngineServiceTests.swift:191`, `DenseGPUEquivalenceTests.swift:34`, `RepackCLITests.swift:220`, `MemoryToolForgetTests.swift:51`), so it is automatic in both directions -- an option added to the parser without a help line fails, and so does a help line for an option nobody reads. What it does not catch is a flag read through a shape that is not a bare quoted literal, and out-of-range numbers are still accepted. Measured on the release binary: `prompt-all --limit 1` against a stub member holding four live sessions reports `considered: 1, delivered: 1` and the stub records 1 prompt, while `--limit 0`, `--limit -1` and no `--limit` at all each report `considered: 4, delivered: 4` with `ok: true` and the stub records 4 -- so a bounded broadcast silently becomes the whole group (`FleetCommands.swift:188`, `if let limit, limit > 0`); `top --width -5` and `--width 0` exit 0 having printed 0 bytes where `--width 80` prints a 30-line frame, and `--height -5` exits 0 with a truncated frame. Nothing in this CLI documents a range for any of them, and inventing one is a behaviour change, not a fix, so that is filed as its own row.

**Commit.** `8a02587`

### AUD-186 — The launcher promised the model survives the client; its own EXIT trap kills it, so the sentence described a lifetime the code refuses to give

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier B
- **Project:** launcher
- **Location:** `tools/server_launcher.sh:1905-1913 (the comment above the client dispatch), checked against the trap at tools/server_launcher.sh:1516-1517`
- **Category:** documentation / a written promise contradicted by the code above it: the claim would license an orphaned model process this project's own precondition forbids
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** Carried from the pre-compaction candidate list and re-read against the current tree rather than filed from memory. The comment above the `case "$CLIENT" in` dispatch said "The model keeps running after the client exits; the next launcher run stops it on this port and starts fresh", while 400 lines earlier the launcher installs `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM` right after starting the server, and `cleanup` kills `$server_pid`. The two cannot both be true. Read at the source: the stale-server stop (server_launcher.sh:1454-1479) is what a *later* run uses to clear a port, so the comment had the mechanism right and the lifetime wrong.

**Evidence before.** Measured with a stub binary so no model was loaded: `TINYTITAN_BIN_DIR` points at a directory holding a python HTTP stub that serves `/v1/models` and writes its pid, `CODEX` at a stub client, on a free port chosen by the test (the real server on this Mac, pid 17514 port 8080, was printed before and after and never touched). `bash tools/server_launcher.sh --answers default --thinking off --ram 4 --engine gpu --concurrency 1 --port <free> --client codex`, stdin "2": launcher exit 0, "fake client ran", and the stub server's pid dead immediately on exit -- the trap fires, the model does not survive. So the behaviour is correct and the comment is the defect. Reach check: the false claim exists only at server_launcher.sh:1907. A whole-tree sweep for the phrasing (keeps running after / stays up after / outlives the client, and the doc-side shapes "server_launcher.*keeps|stays|remain" and "after the client exits") returns no other prose making the promise -- not README.md, not docs/, not the plugins -- so no user-facing document repeats it and no wiki push is owed for this row. The two `wait` paths (`--client server`, server_launcher.sh:1861-1865, and the missing-client path at :1900) were read, not run: both keep the two lifetimes matched the same way. What is NOT verified: the SIGINT/SIGTERM deliveries themselves -- the trap lists all three and the process test drives the ordinary EXIT, so the tested path is the one a person uses by quitting the client, and the signal paths are covered only by reading. No real model process was involved at any point.

**Fix.** The comment now states the lifetime the code gives: the server does not outlive the script, the EXIT/INT/TERM trap fires when the launcher returns, the port is free for the next run, and that is what this project's pre-model precondition asks for -- an orphaned `TinyTitanServer` makes the next gate or golden run refuse to start. The stale-server stop keeps its documented reason, which the old sentence blurred: it exists for a server this script did not start (a bare `swift run`, or a launcher killed with SIGKILL, which no trap can catch). Behaviour is deliberately unchanged: no runtime default, no trap, no signal list was touched. Three tests in the new `benchmark/test_launcher_lifetime.py` pin both halves so a later edit cannot make the claim true by moving the code or false by re-rewriting the prose; the suite is added to CI's installer-and-launcher gates step (`five` -> `six` suites), which names the stub-binary seam so the runner knows no model is loaded.

**Evidence after.** TDD, in that order. All three tests were written first and the prose test failed for the right reason (`/tmp/red186.log`, exit 1, `Ran 3 tests`, `FAILED (failures=1)`): the assertion message quotes the match it found -- `<re.Match object; span=(12, 42), match='keeps running after the client'> is not None : server_launcher.sh promises a lifetime the trap above it does not give` -- while the other two (trap position, real subprocess) passed pre-fix, which is the point: the code already did the right thing. After the comment rewrite the same file is `Ran 3 tests ... OK` (`/tmp/green186.log`), and the sibling launcher suites are `Ran 80 tests ... OK` (`/tmp/green186-sib.log`: ram, port, concurrency, install, coder clients, profile, fixture). Mutation proof that the pins are not decorative (`/tmp/mut186.log`): dropping `EXIT` from the trap makes `test_the_trap_is_installed_before_the_client_runs` FAIL with "no EXIT/INT/TERM cleanup trap in the launcher" and makes `test_the_server_is_gone_when_the_launcher_exits_after_the_client` ERROR at its 180 s timeout, the orphan holding the capture pipe open -- `Ran 3 tests in 180.020s / FAILED (failures=1, errors=1)`. Restored, green again (`/tmp/green186b.log`, `/tmp/green186c.log`). The anchor matters and was chosen deliberately: `case "$CLIENT" in` appears four times in this file (395, 1429, 1771, 1912), so the test locates the dispatch from its `codex)    "$BIN" ;;` arm and takes the last preceding `case`, which is the client dispatch; a naive search pins line 395 and the ordering assertion fails spuriously. Gates: `tools/lint.sh python` (pinned ruff 0.16.7) ok after `ruff format` on the new file, `tools/lint.sh shell` and `shellcheck` (0.11.0) ok for the launcher, the YAML of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` parses and contains `test_launcher_lifetime` in the step's run list, and `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` -- all eighteen gates on the pinned tools -- exit 0 over the tree that became `4bca347`, and re-run over the final tree with this row in it.

**Commit.** `4bca347`

- **Discovered by:** Phase D convergence, sweeping for the AUD-184/AUD-185 class on the surface neither covered -- the server's own request validation. The shape was grepped rather than guessed: `guard let x, x > 0 else { return <default> }` over `sources/`, which returned exactly one wire-fed instance, and it was in the compaction budget. Read at the source first: `targetTokens(maxContext:requested:)` computed `cap = min(4096, max(256, maxContext/8))` and then `guard let requested, requested > 0 else { return cap }`, so a present-but-non-positive value and an absent one produced the same answer; `docs/server-api.md:252` wrote the rule as "(`max_compaction_tokens`, else one eighth of the context, capped at 4096)", where "else" is the sentence for the *absent* case -- the code applied it to the unreadable one too. Unlike the two earlier copies, the positive branch was pinned (`CompactionTests.swift:129-135`, including the deliberate clamp `requested: 900, maxContext: 1_024 -> 512`); the non-positive ones were tested by nothing.

**Evidence before.** Measured through the real route before touching it, using the suite's own `CompactionBackend` (a stub `ServerInferenceBackend` that records every `ValidatedChatRequest`), so no model was loaded (`/tmp/red187b.log`). `{"max_compaction_tokens":0}` -> HTTP 200, a 548-byte body, no `error` envelope, the summariser ran, and the server's own diagnostic line for that request reads `compacted mode=model note_tokens=10 budget=4096`. `{"max_compaction_tokens":-5}` -> the same four things. The positive control in the same run, `{"max_compaction_tokens":256}` -> 200 with `budget=256`, which is what makes the two above a bug rather than a design: the field IS honoured when it is readable, so a caller sending 0 was not getting a documented "0 means default" -- it was getting the default for an omitted field, in answer to a number it had actually set. Reach: `grep` over `plugins/`, `sources/TinyTitanCLI` and `sources/TinyTitanLib` finds no in-tree caller that sends `max_compaction_tokens` (the `dsh-tinytitan` bundle does not use `/v1/responses/compact`), so this is a wire contract for an outside client, exactly as AUD-185 was -- and the same rule still applies, because the compaction endpoint's whole job is to fit a note the caller named. Blast radius is bounded: loopback-only server, no data loss, no crash (the downstream `extractiveSummary` already clamps with `keep = max(0, budget - marker.count)`, ServerCompaction.swift:231-238, so a zero budget could never trap), and the cost of the defect is wasted generation and a note far larger than the caller's window plan. What is NOT verified: no live model compaction was run -- the budget number is computed by the route before the summariser is called, and the stub records exactly what a real backend would receive.

**Fix.** One rule, the AUD-184/AUD-185 rule, applied to the third layer: the route refuses a bound it cannot read, by name, before anything is generated. `HTTPServerHandler+Compact.swift` now throws `ServerRequestError.invalid("max_compaction_tokens must be greater than 0; omit it to let the server choose from the context window", param: "max_compaction_tokens", code: "invalid_value")` for a present, non-positive value -- so the way to get the default is the way the doc already described it, by omitting the field. `targetTokens` keeps its positive floor and its doc comment now states who that floor is for (callers inside this repository; not the answer to a client), and `CompactionRequest.maxCompactionTokens` plus `docs/server-api.md` say the boundary the code finally applies: present means used as sent, clamped only to half the context; zero or negative is a 400. Sibling sweep of the same shape, cleared with the reason: the other `> 0 else { return ... }` hits in `sources/` are internal, not caller-facing -- `RuntimeConfiguration.parseBudgetBytes` (:186-208) returns nil precisely so the caller raises an argument error ("a typo becomes an argument error rather than a silently tiny cache", its own doc) and `expertCacheSlots` (:221) guards a derived stride/layer count; `ContextAssembler.swift:250` returns "include nothing" when there is no room; `SessionLog.swift:426` and `TaskMemory.swift:300` treat `maxBytesPerTask > 0` as "eviction is on", so 0 there means delete nothing -- the fail-safe direction, the same reason AUD-186's `zeroKeepsEverything` memory test is correct and was cleared; and the rest are Metal kernel selection. The other wire bounds were checked in the same pass and already refuse by name: chat `max_tokens` (`maximum > 0` -> invalid, OpenAIRequestValidator.swift:211-226, which also refuses a value over the context rather than clamping it), Anthropic `max_tokens` (AnthropicMapper.swift:330-335) and `thinking.budget_tokens` (:263-274). The guard against recurrence is the two new tests plus the doc line.

**Evidence after.** TDD, in that order. Both tests were written first and the boundary one failed for the right reason (`/tmp/red187b.log`, exit 1): 8 issues, four per value, `response.statusCode == 400` (it was 200), `error != nil` (the body had no error envelope), the `param` assertion, and `backend.log.requests.isEmpty` -- the last one being the proof that the summariser had actually been run for a budget the server could not honor. The positive control passed pre-fix and still does, which is the point: it pins the literal path the refusal depends on. After the guard, the same suite is green (`/tmp/green187.log`, exit 0) and the server logs `budget=4096` only for requests that omitted the field. Mutation proof that both boundary values are really asserted, not just one: replacing `requested > 0` with `requested >= 0` in the new guard fails the first test with 4 issues on the zero case while the negative case still passes (`/tmp/mut187.log`: 4 issues, all of them on the zero case), so a guard that only refused -5 would not survive it; the file was restored and re-verified. `swift test --no-parallel` exit 0 at 1707 tests in 253 suites with zero issue lines (1705 before, plus these two), and `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` -- all eighteen gates on the pinned tools, including swift-format and swiftlint --strict over the four changed Swift files and `docs` over the edited `server-api.md` -- exit 0 over the tree that became `a99dafa`, and again over the final tree with this row in it. No model was loaded at any point; the real `TinyTitanServer` on this Mac (pid 17514, port 8080) was left running and untouched, as it is not this session's process.

### AUD-188 — A turn lost before any content is written was reported by a mechanism nothing tested: of the three journal writes that can lose one, only the content path had a test, so a `record` rewritten to catch locally passed the whole suite

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier B
- **Project:** memory
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityJournalStore.swift:36-41 (`record`'s `guard let taskID = try? await store.taskID(for: scope), let sessionID = … else { return }`), its `session(for:)` at :156-161 (`try? await engine.beginSession`), sources/TinyTitanMemory/MemoryService.swift:136-141 (`recordTurn` asking the engine after every turn), sources/ContinuityCore/ContinuityEngine+Internals.swift:73-81 (`record(_:)`, the write both guards depend on)`
- **Category:** test gap on a deliberate swallow: a `try?` that is honest only because a side channel records the failure and a caller reads it back, with one of its three paths unguarded
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** Phase D convergence, sweeping the swallow-a-write class in the memory subsystem after AUD-187 closed it at the wire. It began as a candidate bug — `record` swallows two failure classes and returns, and `SessionJournal.swift:19-21` invites that reading by promising only that `record` never throws at the caller — and was measured out of that classification before anything changed, which is the reason this row files something smaller than what it set out to find. The report exists and works: every write that can throw records itself on the engine first (`ContinuityEngine+Internals.swift:77` in `record(_:)`, and the session-log observer at :26 for a content event), `ContinuityStore.swift:419` exposes it, and `MemoryService.recordTurn` asks for it after every turn (`_ = await journalFailed(in: session.scope)`, MemoryService.swift:139), which emits `.degraded(operation: "journal", …)` once per workspace (MemoryService+Maintenance.swift:157-165). What was true and unfixed is the other half: the suite had exactly one test over this seam, `aTurnTheJournalRefusesFlipsDurabilityWithoutFailingIt`, and it refuses every record kind at once, so the loss it exercises arrives through the *observer*. Nothing covered the two paths that go through `record(_:)` instead — the task record (`ContinuityStore+KeyMapping.swift:33-46`, whose `createTask` is the only throw in `taskID(for:)`) and the session begin (`:147-151`).

**Evidence before.** Read at the source first, then measured. The measurement corrected the premise, so it is recorded rather than smoothed over: the task guard is *unreachable from the service* for a normally-begun session. A scratch suite refused only the `task` kind from before `engine.start()` and drove two real `recordTurn` calls (`/tmp/probe188.log`, printed `PROBE tasks=0 userPrompts=2 assistantResponses=2`, then deleted): the task record never reached the file — `sessionLog.createTask` mutates RAM before the journal write, so the first `sessionInit` leaves the task in memory even though its record failed, and `task(for:)` takes the `engine.task(id) == nil` branch on the next call — and both turns were journaled anyway. So the loss is the one record, not the session, and the `.degraded` line still fires because the engine had the failure. The reachability that does exist is at the journal itself: a `record` for a scope whose task is not in RAM stops at that guard and drops the turn, and a turn whose session id the memory store never opened (`ContinuityStore.swift:410`, `sessionIDs[id]`, populated by `sessionInit`) has to be begun by the journal, where a refused `.session` write returns nil from `session(for:)` and the turn is gone. Both are real — `ContinuityJournalStore` is `public` and `record` is on the `SessionJournal` protocol, so a caller that holds the journal can reach either — and both were tested by nothing. Against that, the cost of the gap is bounded and it is not data corruption: the curated store's writes still fail loudly (`ContinuityCore` memory observer at ContinuityEngine+Internals.swift:44-46 rethrows `ContinuityError.notPersisted`, so `memory_set` cannot answer "stored" over a refused journal — MemoryJournalFailureTests' own tests), durability flips, and what the swallow protects is the reply the person already has. What is NOT verified: no `FileJournal` on a real disk was involved — the probes run on an in-memory journal double, because `ContinuityEngine.flush()` casts to `FileJournal` and a non-file journal returns early, so a durability *barrier* failure cannot be produced through any injected seam at all; that class is left open in the fix-summary rather than filed on speculation.

**Fix.** No behaviour changed, and the row says so: what was missing was the guard, not the code. Two tests pin the two uncovered paths, in the file that already owns the seam (`tests/TinyTitanMemory/MemoryJournalFailureTests.swift`): `aTurnLostToAFailedTaskRecordIsStillReported` (the turn is gone, the engine holds the failure, and the *next* turn of the same workspace journals normally — which documents that the swallow costs one turn, not the workspace) and `aTurnLostToAFailedSessionRecordIsStillReported` (the task write succeeded, so the refusal can only be felt at the session; the turn is gone, the failure is recorded, and reading the session back gives an honest empty rather than a swallowed one). To make them separate paths rather than one scenario twice, `RefusingJournal` gained a record-kind selector — refusing everything cannot tell the three ways a turn is lost apart. The comment on `record` now names the mechanism the `try?` depends on (the engine records before it throws; `recordTurn` asks), because that invariant is what makes the swallow acceptable and it is exactly the thing a reader of `guard … else { return }` cannot see. Sibling sweep of every `try?` in `sources/ContinuityCore`, each cleared with its reason: ContinuityEngine+Internals.swift:70 `try? await compactJournal()` — compaction writes to a `.compacting` temp and renames (Journal.swift:354-372), so a failure throws before the live file is touched and nothing is lost; and if the reopen at :386 fails, the descriptor is -1 and `writeFully` then throws `EBADF` (:216), so the state is loud on the next append rather than quiet. ContinuityEngine.swift:221 `recordMemoryWrite` and :331 `recordContextAssembled`, SessionLog.swift:114 `completeAssistantResponse` — structural log events (`carriesContent` returns false for both kinds, :54-63); the fact or the reply itself is journaled by a different observer, so losing them loses explanation, not memory. Journal.swift:202 `Task.sleep` — a backoff. :400, :413, :424 `removeItem(at: temporary)` — cleanup of a file that is either committed or abandoned. :454-455 `settleBarrier`/`performBarrier` inside `truncate()` and `shutDown()`, and ContinuityEngine.swift:127 `journal.shutDown()` — the descriptor is going away. Two stay open, and they are open because they cannot be measured rather than because they look fine: `try? await flush()` at ContinuityEngine.swift:106 (end of session) and :125 (shutdown), and the deferred barrier at Journal.swift:205 — `sync()` really can throw (`F_FULLFSYNC` then `fsync` both fail, :254-258), and such a failure is not routed to `journalWriteFailed`, so a workspace would keep reporting itself durable after the one operation whose job was to make it so. No seam on this host makes `fsync` fail, and filing it on reading alone would be the thing this audit keeps correcting; it is recorded here as the next thing to try to reproduce, together with the reason the attempt has to be made against a `FileJournal` on a real volume. The named guard against recurrence is the two tests, and the kind selector that lets a future path be refused on its own.

**Evidence after.** TDD in the order the finding allowed. These are coverage tests, so they were expected to pass against the unmodified code — and the honest proof is not that but that they can fail, which was measured: removing `journalWriteFailed(error)` from `ContinuityEngine.record(_:)` (the report the swallow depends on) fails both new tests on `failure != nil` and leaves the four older ones green (`/tmp/mut188.log`) — the older content-path test survives because it goes through the session-log observer, which is the very distinction this row turns on. The file was restored and the suite re-run. The first version of the task test asserted a service-level scenario, and the measurement above showed the premise was wrong; it was rewritten against the journal rather than adjusted until it went green. `swift test --no-parallel` exit 0 at 1709 tests in 253 suites with zero issue lines (`/tmp/suite188.log`, 1707 before plus these two), and `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over the final tree (`/tmp/lint188b.log`). It did not pass first time: the `all` run failed the swift-format gate on a wrapped `#expect` in the new test (`/tmp/lint188.log`), which was fixed with the toolchain's own `swift-format` on that one file and re-verified, not hand-tuned. No model was loaded; the real `TinyTitanServer` on this Mac (pid 17514, port 8080) was left running and untouched, as it is not this session's process.

### AUD-191 — The C kernels document a bitwise agreement between the 4-bit and 8-bit widths that they do not have, and no test measured the claim

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier A
- **Project:** engine
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/include/tinytitan_kernels.h:17-24 and :37-44 (the two entry-point docs that said the widths 'round alike'), sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/int8_affine_gemv.c:9-13 (the 'deliberately parallel' header) and :104-115 (the reduction comment above `(d0+d1)+(d2+d3)`, now :116)`
- **Category:** documentation claim stronger than the code, in a file with zero ledger coverage -- the class this audit kept finding, now in the kernels rather than the Swift
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** Phase D convergence, on the first pass over `sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/`, which no earlier row had touched. The prompt was the one that found AUD-189 and AUD-190: read a comment that states a property and ask whether anything asserts it. `int8_affine_gemv.c` said the 4-bit kernel's single accumulator and this one's four 'reduce to the same value for the same inputs', and `tinytitan_kernels.h` said both widths 'round alike at group boundaries'. Reading `int4_affine_gemv.c` showed why that cannot be: every int4 lane chains all sixteen of its products into one `float32x4`, while int8 keeps four and combines them as `(d0+d1)+(d2+d3)`.

**Evidence before.** Three measurements, the first in the committed test and two by scratch C probes against the real kernels. (1) RED, the test asserting the claimed identity: `Expectation failed: four == eight` -- 4-bit `[955.4322, 955.4322, 955.4322]` against 8-bit `[955.43225, 955.43225, 955.43225]` for the same 256 products, scale BF16 1.0, bias 0.0, exit 1, 1 issue. (2) 400,000 randomized rows through both C entry points: 256,735 bitwise mismatches, 64.1838%, and the probe exits 1 on any mismatch. (3) 80,000 rows at the same scale, checked against a double-precision reference: 51,605 mismatches (64.51%), worst relative error 1.844e-03 for int4 and 2.570e-03 for int8; re-run with unit-scale `x` at 80,000 rows: 55,094 mismatches (68.87%), 1.060e-02 and 3.835e-03. So both widths are right to well under a percent of the row and differ in the last bits, exactly as the reduction orders predict. What nothing showed was a consumer of the stronger claim: no CPU golden target exists (`benchmark/golden/` is GPU greedy generation), the side-engine is validated against `tools/qwen35_reference.py` rather than against the other width, and no test compares a CPU row to a Metal row -- `docs/v4.4-decode-width-plan.md:552` already documents CPU/GPU agreement as 'to a rounding error', which is the same fact the kernels' own headers denied.

**Fix.** The three claims now say what is true: the two kernels share the *factoring* `scale * sum(q*x) + bias * sum(x)` per group, which is the contract, and the reduction inside a group is not shared, so reordering one kernel moves the last bits of its own width instead of breaking an exact agreement between the widths. No numerics changed -- the accumulators and their order are untouched, which is the rule in `AGENTS.md` (do not alter numerics unless asked). The test is replaced with the honest assertion: `bothWidthsAgreeToWithinARoundingErrorNotBitForBit` feeds identical products to both widths through `CPUOps.gemv`, the wrapper the engine itself calls, and bounds each row's gap by that row's own total absolute magnitude (`1e-6 * sum(|w|*|x|)`) rather than by the row's value, because a fp32 sum that cancels cannot bound its own roundings. `matchesTheFourBitReferenceOnRepresentableValues` is renamed from `agreesWithTheFourBitPathOnRepresentableValues` and re-documented: it dequantises at 4 bits in Swift and checks the 8-bit kernel against that oracle, so it never compared two kernels at all, and its old name plus doc ('it is why the two kernels factor the accumulation identically') read as if it did.

**Evidence after.** GREEN: `Test run with 7 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.196 seconds`. Mutation, so the new test is proved to be measuring the claim and not the ambient tolerance: `vzipq_u8(lo, hi)` -> `vzipq_u8(hi, lo)` in `int4_affine_gemv.c` (swapping which nibble is element 2k, i.e. changing the products the 4-bit kernel pairs) produced `row 0: gap 0.6291504 over 0.00095543225 (954.8031 vs 955.43225)` and the file was then restored -- `git diff --stat` on it empty. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel`, exit 0: 1712 tests in 253 suites across the 7 targets, 0 failures (`/tmp/suite191.log`) -- one test more than AUD-190's 1711/253, which is this one. `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH tools/lint.sh all`, exit 0 across all eighteen gates (`/tmp/lint191.log`); `test-hollow` now counts 1686 bodies, up from 1685, none hollow. Sibling sweep, in the order the sweep found them: (1) `int4_affine_gemv.c` re-read whole -- its header makes no cross-width claim at all (it is about why the C loop beats the Swift one, and about the mask/shift/zip unpack), so the only false statements were the two in the 8-bit file and the pair in the shared header, and nothing in the 4-bit kernel needed changing; (2) `tinytitan_kernels.h` scanned for every other equality-shaped phrase -- the remaining ones are about the affine *format* (one BF16 scale and one bias per 64 elements) and about element packing, both of which the tests do pin; (3) the `moe.metal` SIMD row (`moe_affine_gemv_row_simd`, :515-599) owns elements differently per lane (`e = g*64 + lane*2`) and reduces with `simd_sum`, so CPU-vs-GPU is the same story one level up -- **not filed**, because nothing claims bitwise identity there; the plan document already states the tolerance, and adding a CPU-to-Metal bitwise test would assert a property the design does not promise. Not verified, and recorded rather than glossed: no model was loaded, so `tools/golden-baseline.sh --check` and `LibraryContractTests` remain **not checked** for this change; they cannot be run against a CPU-only comment-and-test diff anyway, and neither was any kernel source modified. Residual: the 64-69% figure is measured on pseudorandom `x` at the widths' own toy geometry (256 columns), not on a shipping tensor -- the direction of the finding does not depend on it, but a future row that needs the rate should re-measure at real shapes.

**Commit.** `c7e2159`

### AUD-193 — A wrong-typed field in a well-formed JSON body was answered "malformed JSON request" with no parameter, throwing away the name the decoder had already computed

- **Severity / tier:** S3 / Tier A
- **Project:** server
- **Location:** `sources/TinyTitanServer/Core/HTTPServerHandler+Chat.swift:129-135 and its four siblings (+Anthropic.swift:205 and :260, +Responses.swift:179, +Compact.swift:103) -- every generic `catch` that fabricates `malformed JSON request` / `invalid_json` from nothing but the fact that a decode threw`
- **Category:** an error that names the wrong cause: the client is sent to its serializer for a payload whose syntax was never the problem
- **Status:** DONE
- **Host:** Mac (primary)
- **Discovered by:** Phase D convergence, sweeping the request error surfaces for a guard that discards information it was handed. The shape was found by asking what the generic `catch` at the end of each JSON route actually knows: it catches `Error`, so a `DecodingError` -- which carries a `codingPath` naming the exact failing field -- is collapsed to one constant string.

**Evidence before.** RED, measured against the live loopback server (TinyTitanHTTPServer on port 0, real URLSession POST): a body of {"model":"test-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":"abc"} -- valid JSON, wrong type -- answered HTTP 400 with {"error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","code":"invalid_json","message":"malformed JSON request"}} and no param. The new test recorded: Test aWrongTypedFieldInValidJSONNamesTheParameter() recorded an issue at tests/TinyTitanServer/HTTPServerTests.swift:426:9 -- Expectation failed: (param: nil) == "max_tokens". The same collapse was on all five JSON routes, and the Anthropic Messages route folded the missing param into its message string, so the client got the wrong cause in both formats.

**Fix.** RequestDecodingFailure.serverError(_:body:) (62 lines, new file) tells the two client bugs apart: a DecodingError whose bytes are not a JSON document at all (re-parsed with JSONSerialization .fragmentsAllowed, affordable because this only runs on a request already being refused) keeps invalid_json / "malformed JSON request"; everything else becomes invalid_value with the decoder's own codingPath rendered in the dotted form the validators already use (messages.0.content), and a non-DecodingError or an empty path gets the honest nameless wording under @unknown default. Wired into all five generic decode catch sites -- handleCompletion, handleCompact, handleResponses, handleMessages, handleCountTokens -- with the two envelope sites routing through .envelope and the three writeRequestError sites keeping their own surface and requestID, so each format still answers in its own object shape. Not covered, deliberately: ServerCompaction.decode already names param "input" with its own code, and a base64 envelope's codingPath would name a field the client cannot see.

**Evidence after.** GREEN: the four wire tests pass -- swift test --no-parallel --filter on HTTPServerTests gave "Test run with 3 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.041 seconds", and the 600-level-nesting body gave "Test run with 1 test in 1 suite passed after 0.043 seconds". max_tokens now arrives as param "max_tokens" with code invalid_value; {not json still gives invalid_json; the Anthropic route names max_tokens in its message and no longer says "malformed JSON request". Full serial suite exit 0: 1718 tests in 253 suites across seven test runs, 0 failures (1714 at b5e0c4e, plus exactly these four). PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH ./tools/lint.sh all exit 0, all 18 gates. Mutation check that the syntax pin is not vacuous: replacing the re-parse guard with `if false` so every decode failure takes the named-parameter branch made the non-JSON tests fail observably -- body was {"error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","code":"invalid_value","message":"request body does not match this endpoint"}}, 2 issues recorded -- and the file was restored afterwards (grep -c "if false" returns 0, swift-format and swiftlint --strict clean).
